questions.q: How does reinforcement learning differ from the supervised models used earlier in this course?
options: An RL agent learns from sequential rewards for actions taken in an environment, rather than being given labeled examples to predict directly
RL requires no data of any kind
RL can only be used for classification, never regression
RL and supervised learning are mathematically identical
questions.explain: Supervised learning predicts a given label from features. Reinforcement learning instead has an agent take sequential actions and learn from reward feedback which actions tend to pay off.

questions.q: In the Markov Decision Process framing of trading, what does the 'reward' typically represent?
options: The number of trades executed per day
Profit and loss over some horizon, often shaped to be risk-adjusted
The number of features in the state representation
The agent's training loss value
questions.explain: The reward is the feedback signal the agent receives after acting, commonly profit-and-loss, often shaped (e.g., penalizing drawdowns) rather than using raw P&L alone.

questions.q: What is the key difference between Q-learning/DQN and policy-gradient methods?
options: Q-learning/DQN learns a value function over state-action pairs and acts greedily on it; policy-gradient methods learn the policy directly
Policy-gradient methods cannot be used for trading
Q-learning only works with continuous actions
There is no meaningful difference between the two approaches
questions.explain: Q-learning/DQN estimates expected future reward for state-action pairs and picks the best-estimated action. Policy-gradient methods instead learn the action-choosing policy directly, which tends to suit continuous action spaces better.

questions.q: Why is building a realistic training simulation such a difficult part of RL for trading?
options: Simulations are illegal to use in finance

RL agents need far more interactions than real market history provides, so training happens in simulation, which must realistically capture market impact and transaction costs or the learned policy will fail live
Simulations always run slower than real markets
Simulated environments cannot be coded in Python
questions.explain: Because real market history can't supply enough interactions for RL training, simulation is usually required -- and if that simulation doesn't realistically model market impact and transaction costs, the agent learns a policy that looks good on paper but fails in live trading.

questions.q: What is the lesson's overall framing of reinforcement learning for trading?
options: A mature, production-ready solution that should replace supervised models
A genuinely hard, still largely research-stage area -- promising for narrower problems like optimal trade execution, but not an off-the-shelf solution
A technique that has been fully solved and is no longer studied
A method that only works for cryptocurrency trading
questions.explain: The lesson frames RL for trading as an active research area with real promise for specific, narrower applications like optimal execution, but not something to deploy with the same confidence as the supervised models covered earlier in the course.
